paragraphs: Rain fell on Jingkou for three days without stopping, hiding even the summit of Mount Suan. The river was a blur of gray. From time to time half a sail emerged from the rain, only to vanish again in the wind. Outside the Northern Garrison’s camp gate, a grain cart sank into a muddy rut. Six soldiers heaved at ropes and shouted in rhythm, but the wheel had risen barely half an inch when the sacks at the back began to tumble. A hemp rope snapped, and sticky black millet spilled over the ground, mingling with yellow water.

The shipping clerk from Jiankang hastily planted his foot against the torn sack and ordered the grain taken into storage. Shen Shi of the Seventh Battalion picked out a few grains, smelled them, and threw them into the mud. “We’d be better off swallowing sand with river water than eating this.”

The clerk stood beneath an umbrella beside the cart, his boots spotless. At the remark he immediately ordered someone to write down Shen Shi’s name. An officer came from behind the tents, an old straw rain cape pulled over his armor, the mouth of his sword scabbard worn pale in a ring. Liu Yu did not begin by asking who was quarrelling. He took a sack, slit the seam, and let little stones and empty husks pour out. Rain dimpled the heap of millet until it looked like a festering wound.
“How much does this cart claim to carry?” he asked.
“Eight hundred shi. Inspected and certified by the Jiankang Finance Granary.”

“So this is how badly they dare adulterate it after inspection?” Liu Yu ordered the soldiers to bring out the scales and stack the spoiled grain separately beneath the gallery. The clerk shouted that he had unlawfully opened government stores and stirred up disorder among the troops. Liu Yu told him only to put those accusations in the record as well. As the clerk stormed out of camp, Shen Shi lowered his voice. “Captain Liu, you’ll be getting the rod for this.”
“We haven’t finished weighing,” Liu Yu said, sheathing his sword. “A beating won’t feed anybody.”

At headquarters, Liu Laozhi had already received the complaint. He asked his staff officer whether anyone had inspected the grain. More than two hundred sacks had been opened, the officer replied. Three in ten were moldy, two in ten contained sand and stones, and the rest was barely edible. At the ration allowance for the whole camp, it would not last two days. Liu Laozhi laid the red-sealed receipt marked “eight hundred shi” on his desk without showing anger. At the other end of the desk lay three edicts newly arrived from Jiankang. Their paper was fresh and so was the sealing wax, yet each was harder to obey than the last.

One ordered three thousand elite Northern Garrison soldiers into Jiankang to guard the palace. Another directed that pay be suspended for all troops whose families had crossed north, pending investigation and disposition. The third demanded that the command choose five thousand soldiers within ten days to march south to Kuaiji, with the camp to supply their provisions in advance. Liu Laozhi turned the documents over and over. At last he asked, “Has the finance office sent even one shi of fresh grain?”
“No.”

Hasty footsteps sounded outside. An investigating officer from Jiankang had arrived with a supposed case of collusion with Qin. Jiang Shun, an old soldier of the Ninth Battalion, possessed a family letter written under a Qin guest registration. His mother, wife, children, and grandchildren had crossed the Huai by night half a month earlier, and a local Qin official was prepared to attest to their arrival. The investigator requested execution at noon, the head to be displayed at the camp gate as a warning to all other military households.

Liu Laozhi ordered Jiang Shun and Liu Yu brought together to the drill ground. Jiang Shun was past forty, with a piece missing from his left ear, a wound suffered years ago while guarding the northern bank. Rain ran from his hair into his eyes, but he did not wipe it away. The stake for the execution was already set, and a ring-pommeled sword lay on a wooden tray. Beside it a military clerk held the service roll, waiting to strike through a name entered there for seventeen years.

As the investigator read the charge, Liu Yu demanded the evidence. He examined the letter and saw that most of it had been written by a hired scribe. The last few crooked lines, however, were in a woman’s own hand: on the north bank, a medical officer had seen to the sick child; their grandson could swallow a great bowl of millet porridge; you are still serving in the Jin army, so do not throw your life away because we escaped here. There was no map of Qin deployments, no frontier cipher, not a single word urging surrender.
“His wife and children have fled to Qin territory. Is that not collusion with the enemy?” the investigator demanded.
“A soldier’s offense must be proved against the soldier,” Liu Yu replied, folding the letter. “Of all the forts he has guarded for seventeen years, which one has ever been reported lost?”
“Then why did he hide the letter?”
Jiang Shun suddenly lifted his head. “Because I was afraid.”

Liu Laozhi asked what he feared. Jiang Shun swallowed a mouthful of rain and said he was afraid they would find his family and bring them back by force. The investigator said Qin land lay far away; who could possibly seize them there? Jiang Shun looked at him and answered that when the Zhou clan of Guangling had taken his family’s twelve mu of military farmland, all they had needed was a sheet of paper. That land had been awarded for his military service. For three years he had been unable to return and cultivate it because he was guarding the walls; county officials declared it unattended and transferred it to the Zhous for their estate. His wife was beaten for lodging a petition. Their youngest son fell ill, and with no money for a physician he died at home. When the grain ran out too, the old mother led the family across the river.

“Why didn’t I go home for three years?” Jiang Shun suddenly strained against his guards, who for a moment failed to hold him down. “Because the Qin army hadn’t withdrawn from the north, and the court ordered us to stand fast! We stood until our family land had become the Zhou clan’s wasteland, stood until my child was dead. And now they tell me my family are traitors!”

A line of soldiers stood in silence. Some wore bandages around their hands; others had just returned from north of the river, with water still inside their boots. Until now Jiang Shun’s troubles had been his alone, but many men now remembered the land deeds they had handed to their relatives before marching away. The investigator twice shouted for the guards to hold Jiang Shun down. No one stepped forward at once.
Liu Laozhi came down from the gallery with his cloak around his shoulders and stood before Jiang Shun. “If Qin soldiers cross the Yangtze one day, will you fight them or not?”

Jiang Shun looked across the drill ground toward the Jin banner, heavy with rain and plastered against its pole. “I will. My family survived in Qin country; I won’t forget that. But if Qin soldiers come to take a city I am guarding, I cannot hand it over to them.”
“Trying to serve both sides!” the investigator sneered.

Liu Yu could bear listening no longer. “He still wears Northern Garrison armor, and if he falls in battle he’ll be entered on the Jin army’s list of dead. If the mere wish to keep one’s wife and children alive counts as treason, where will we find men willing to defend our cities?”

The investigator pointed at Liu Yu and promised to report his words to the Prince of Kuaiji. Liu Yu did not lower his head. But Liu Laozhi barked at him to step back. They faced each other a moment; Liu Yu saluted his general and at last retreated half a pace.

Liu Laozhi took the edict from the investigator himself. He saw that it ordered only an inquiry into military households. It did not explicitly command immediate execution, nor did it show that Jiang Shun had divulged military intelligence to Qin. If the man died now, the Jiankang envoy’s task would be neatly dispatched; the men left in camp, however, would learn that any soldier with family north of the Huai could be driven to the wall. Liu Laozhi announced that Jiang Shun was reprieved pending inquiry. The letter would be retained as evidence and the old Guangling deeds and military-merit rolls investigated. Yet Liu Yu’s unauthorized opening of military grain and public quarrel with the envoy could not be ignored under military law either.

The clerk writing at the side had begun to tremble. The investigator declared that he would report the affair truthfully. Liu Laozhi told him to include the general’s own signature. Then he ordered his guards to escort the envoy to the post house and keep him inside camp until the circumstances were fully recorded. Was he putting a court envoy under arrest? the man demanded furiously. With thieves active on the waterways around Jingkou, Liu Laozhi answered, headquarters had a duty to protect an envoy’s safety. The man glared with hatred, but he knew he had come with no more than a handful of attendants.

Before the whole camp, Liu Yu submitted to thirty strokes of the rod. At the fifteenth blow Liu Laozhi ordered a halt, with the remaining strokes to be entered in the military register. He offered Liu Yu no praise and did not treat the punishment as a performance staged for Jiankang. If a captain could break open a sealed government grain store without consequences, tomorrow another man might assemble troops to seize provisions under the pretext of defending their interests. But at the same time the general ordered the entire eight hundred shi reexamined. The moldy grain and stones were to be bagged again and returned to Jiankang. Cart numbers, seals, and the names of every person who had handled the shipment were to be copied without omission into the memorial.

Shen Shi washed Liu Yu’s wounded back. As he cut away the wet tunic he saw old scars across the shoulder running into fresh blood. He cursed Liu Laozhi under his breath. Liu Yu told him to apply the medicine more gently and, after a long pause, said, “If the general hadn’t given me even those fifteen strokes, next time Jiankang would claim I led men in to plunder the grain. We still haven’t finished examining the accounts that need examining.”

Shen Shi was unconvinced. Jiang Shun’s family had gone north and at least those people received grain. Why keep starving at Jingkou? Liu Yu watched water drip from the roof of the tent and remembered his own childhood, poor, ill, and without anyone to rely on, when borrowing grain had so often brought looks of contempt. He had never been to Qin territory, he said, and did not know whether every decree there truly reached the families it was meant to help. But Jiang Shun’s family had been able to send a letter saying they were alive. That fact could not be made to disappear.
“Then why not go?” Shen Shi asked.

“Because the land here belongs to people too, and the soldiers who died along the Huai were soldiers of Jin.” Liu Yu turned painfully onto his side. “Leaving is easy enough. If you stay, somebody has to ask where the grain went.”

At dusk Liu Laozhi summoned him to the riverbank. Mist drifted among the mooring ropes. The farther shore was invisible, and the bows of boats gently knocked together in the fog. The general still held the three Jiankang edicts. Would Liu Yu select five hundred men and go first to Kuaiji, he asked, to discover whether the gathering of refugees there really had been caused by harsh taxes and compulsory labor? Liu Yu did not accept at once. First he asked how many days the grain stores could last. Then he asked what would become of the pay suspended for Jiang Shun.
Liu Laozhi looked at him. “A mere captain like you proposes to audit the accounts of my headquarters?”
“If I go to Kuaiji, my general, someone must watch them here for me.”

The river wind whipped Liu Laozhi’s robe. He said he had heard the talk that the Northern Garrison had no master now. Xie An and Xie Xuan were both dead. Jiankang wanted the troops to fight, but feared the power they possessed; the local authorities wanted them to defend the fields, while those taking the fields had married into the great families at court. To say the army had no master was not necessarily to say there was no one holding a command seal. There were several seals. Each demanded the men’s blood, yet scarcely one would make good the pay owed to the camp.

“You tell the soldiers spoiled grain cannot be eaten,” Liu Laozhi said. “If tomorrow every sack is replaced, and the Zhou family of Guangling returns Jiang Shun’s land, will you still be willing to march?”
“Yes.”
“Why?”
“If an army invades, we have to defend ourselves,” Liu Yu said. “But if we’re ordered to march so one great house can win a struggle for position, I’d like to read what that order says first.”
Liu Laozhi laughed despite himself. When the laughter faded, only weariness remained. “So now you’re choosing which military orders to obey.”

He held out the edict concerning Kuaiji. Liu Yu took it and bowed his thanks for the command. The general added that Jiang Shun could be housed for the time being with the wounded soldiers, that a separate memorial would be opened on his family’s land, and that overdue pay would be issued in advance from headquarters' private stores. This time there was enough for three months; next time he might not be able to find it. Liu Yu knew no further questioning would produce more grain, so he offered no grand words. As he turned to leave, however, he stopped. “General, men in camp are waiting for the grain-inspection record you made today.”
“What of it?”
“Let them know they can use it to check the next shipment too.”

That night the battalions of the Northern Garrison took turns inspecting the grain store, its ledgers spread beneath the lamplight. Wounded as he was, Liu Yu made the rounds. He found Shen Shi and several soldiers fiercely disputing how much moldy millet should be deducted from one sack, their faces red with argument, yet not one of them dared slip an extra entry into the account. He ordered sample bags kept sealed beneath the eaves of headquarters so every man could see what Jiankang had sent them.

A young soldier asked what use the records were if the court again refused to acknowledge them. Liu Yu considered, then said only that grain was something they ate every day. They could not wait until men fell on the battlefield to reckon its cost. As for who would acknowledge the evidence in future, he made no empty promise. The night watch drum sounded. From the Seventh to the Ninth Battalion, men rose in sequence and dispersed toward the ration cauldrons of their respective camps.

Liu Yu went to the cauldron, took a bowl of millet, and tasted it first before telling Shen Shi to serve the rest. After the rain, Jingkou smelled of wet earth; the river wind tilted the lantern flames. The next grain boat was still on its way, and the five hundred men due to march south had not all been mustered. The bowl was hot in Liu Yu’s hand. He shifted it to the other and waited for the second cauldron to boil.
